newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices dip on hopeful Iraqi oil sale talk.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices dip on hopeful Iraqi oil sale talk.

text.p: World oil prices were slightly weaker on Monday as profit-taking and positive comments about the Iraqi "oil-for-food" deal by a top U.N. official stalled last week's rally.
But most traders saw Monday's easing as temporary, saying they expected oil prices to resume their ascent in the near future, propelled primarily by strength in heating oil.
At 1640 GMT, benchmark Brent November crude futures, which gained $1.50 last week, were trading 12 cents down on the day at $23.35 a barrel.

United Nations Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi told a news conference in Geneva he hoped the oil-for-food agreement could be implemented "in the near future", adding later that it might be "a matter of weeks".

Most players dismissed Akashi's comments, saying implementation of the deal this year was highly unlikely. But his words served to remind them that as much as 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi oil exports could hit the market once the deal is implmented.

Oil analysts had expected to see as early as this month the first Iraqi oil exports in more than six years after Baghdad was hit by crippling sanctions. But the plan was suspended when President Saddam Hussein sent troops into Kurdish areas in northern Iraq at the beginning of September.
"I don't think many in the market take Akashi's comments seriously, but it cooled futures off a bit," one trader said.

"The market would hardly have noticed such a comment a few months ago, but the Iraqi oil issue has been off the menu for a while and the market has become sensitive to it again," Tim Holmes at oil brokers MeesPierson said.
The oil-for-food plan would have allowed Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months.

But the fact that heating oil stocks in Europe and the United States are at historic lows ahead of the northern hemisphere winter has kept prices around five-year highs for the past two weeks, and traders do not see the situation getting any slacker.
"There has been a bit of profit-taking today but fundamentally the market is very strong," one trader said.
"It's not a market where you want to be short. You get smacked in the face every time," another trader said.
